title: Kunti repays the house
hookLine: in hiding at Ekachakra, Kunti hears her hosts weeping over whose turn it is to die, and offers her own son: a guest's debt, paid as dharma
carry: repaying kindness is dharma, not a favor
last: BHAKTI ASKS FOR GOD OVER COMFORT.

cards: Through a thin wall, in a borrowed room, a mother hears another family crying.
Years before the war, after the house of lac burned, Kunti and her sons are hiding in a town called Ekachakra, dressed as poor brahmins, living with a brahmin family who took them in.
One evening the house fills with weeping. Kunti goes to find out why. Tomorrow, the family tells her, it's their turn.
A demon named Baka lives near the town, and each household in turn must send him a cart of food and a person to be eaten with it. Now they're arguing over who should go. Today: what Kunti says next.

teach.b: The scene is in the Mahabharata's first book, and it starts with the family. The father says he will go. The mother says no, she will; the children need their father more.
The daughter says send me. And the small son picks up a blade of grass, waves it, and says he'll kill the demon with that. Then Kunti speaks, in paraphrase.
You have sheltered us; let me repay you. I have five sons, and one of them will take the food to Baka. The brahmin refuses.
He can't let a guest die for him. Kunti insists: the son she has in mind is strong. When the brothers come home, Yudhishthira is upset: you're risking our brother on a stranger's trouble?
Kunti is calm. She has seen Bhima's strength since he was a baby. And repaying the people who sheltered them, she says, is dharma.
So Bhima goes, eats the demon's food in front of him to make him angry, and kills him. Here's the teaching. Hinduism has a word for what Kunti is weighing: rina, debt.

teach.h: RINA: THE DEBTS WE'RE BORN WITH
teach.b: The Vedic texts say a person is born owing debts, to the gods, to the sages, to the ancestors; and the householder's daily duties include caring for people, the guest above all. Kunti is the guest here, and she owes.
To her, paying it back isn't generosity she can skip.
It's dharma. Her eldest questions her. The decision is hers.

how: Hindus meet the Ekachakra story in retellings of the Mahabharata, in children's books and in storytelling, often told as Bhima's adventure, with Kunti's choice at its center.

o: a mother who hides her sons and lets the town suffer
a queen who orders the brahmin family to go instead
the guest who repays her hosts and calls it dharma

games.q: the night at Ekachakra — tap the pairs.
p: a debt, owed to gods, sages, ancestors

s: Kunti sends Bhima without telling anyone
she tells the brahmin, and Yudhishthira questions her when the brothers come home.
Kunti says repaying the people who sheltered them is dharma
they were guests; she offers a son to repay the house.
the brahmin is glad to let his guest's son go in his place
he refuses at first; he can't let a guest die for him.

games.q: a family took you in during a hard year. now they're in trouble. by Kunti's dharma, what fits?
o: repay them. a guest's debt to the house is dharma.
stay out of it. you were only a guest.
help only if they ask you to.
games.why: Kunti didn't wait to be asked. she offered a son, insisted when the brahmin refused, and told Yudhishthira that repaying the house was dharma.

practice: Bring to mind a time someone took you in, a room, a meal, a ride, a hand when you needed it, and let their face come clearly. Hold them with each breath.

Then let one small way to repay that kindness come to mind, a call, a meal, an hour of help, the way Hindu families have long answered kindness with food and time. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Kunti. In hiding at Ekachakra, she offered one of her own sons to repay the family who sheltered them, and called it dharma. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: born Pritha, raised by King Kuntibhoja, and called Kunti for him. Arjuna is called Partha, Pritha's son.

carryVoice: Your line: repaying kindness is dharma, not a favor. Kunti owed the house. Go gently.
